sources: NCIEA LPF 5-8 NO, PRF, and SE strands — structural source for construct_id (nciea.org/wp-content/uploads/2022/07/Math_LPF_KH11.pdf)
DLM Grade 6-7 Essential Elements — M.EE.6.NS.1, M.EE.6.RP.1, M.EE.7.RP.1 (dynamiclearningmaps.org)
Lamon 5-interpretation fraction LP (part-whole / quotient / measurement / ratio / operator)
_meta.notes: construct_id values must exist in config/knowledge_graph.yaml. Phone-plan entries are keyed to the LPF PRF constructs added in KG v2. detection_patterns are regex used by deterministic expert_slip/persona checks; semantic paraphrase matching over misconception_instances is future work.

misconceptions.source: DLM M.EE.6.NS.1 — IP/DP linkage level; LPF M.NO-1
misconceptions.description: Student treats fraction as two unrelated whole numbers. Concludes 1/4 > 1/3 because 4 > 3.
misconceptions.example_wrong_reply: 1/4 is bigger because 4 is bigger than 3.
misconceptions.prompt_cue: You see the denominator as just a regular number and bigger means more.

misconceptions.source: DLM M.EE.6.NS.1 — DP linkage; LPF M.NO-2
misconceptions.description: Student adds both numerators and denominators independently (2/5 + 1/5 = 3/10).
misconceptions.example_wrong_reply: 2 plus 1 is 3 and 5 plus 5 is 10, so 3/10.
misconceptions.prompt_cue: You add the top numbers together AND the bottom numbers together just like regular addition.

misconceptions.source: DLM M.EE.6.NS.1 — DP/PP boundary; LPF M.NO-2
misconceptions.description: To subtract fractions, student subtracts numerators and denominators directly. 5/6 - 1/3 = 4/3.
misconceptions.example_wrong_reply: 5 minus 1 is 4, 6 minus 3 is 3, answer is 4/3.
misconceptions.prompt_cue: You subtract the top from the top and the bottom from the bottom, just like you do with addition.

misconceptions.source: DLM M.EE.6.NS.1 — PP linkage level
misconceptions.description: Student identifies the LCD correctly but converts the fraction incorrectly (1/3 → 1/6 instead of 2/6).
misconceptions.example_wrong_reply: LCD is 6. So 1/3 becomes 1/6. 5/6 minus 1/6 equals 4/6.
misconceptions.prompt_cue: You know you need the same bottom number but you forget to multiply the top when you change the bottom.

misconceptions.source: LPF M.NO-2 — Successor level skill
misconceptions.description: Correct computation but student does not simplify (e.g. leaves answer as 3/6 instead of 1/2).
misconceptions.example_wrong_reply: 5/6 minus 2/6 equals 3/6.
misconceptions.prompt_cue: You get the right fraction but simplifying feels unnecessary to you — the answer looks fine.

misconceptions.source: DLM M.EE.6.RP.1 — PP linkage (1:n ratio)
misconceptions.description: Student reverses ratio order (blue:red instead of red:blue).
misconceptions.example_wrong_reply: The ratio is 5:2 because there are 5 blue and 2 red.
misconceptions.prompt_cue: You write the numbers in the order you see them or say them, not the order asked.

misconceptions.source: Lamon fraction-as-ratio interpretation; LPF M.NO-1
misconceptions.description: Student expresses ratio as part-to-whole (2:7) instead of part-to-part (2:5).
misconceptions.example_wrong_reply: 2 red out of 7 total, so 2:7.
misconceptions.prompt_cue: You compare each part to the whole, not to the other part.

misconceptions.source: DLM M.EE.6.RP.1 — T linkage
misconceptions.description: Student gives correct notation but treats ratio as a fraction without multiplicative meaning.
misconceptions.example_wrong_reply: 2/5, like a fraction.
misconceptions.prompt_cue: You write 2/5 because it looks like a fraction. You don't think about it as a comparison between two groups.

misconceptions.source: LPF M.NO.2d (additive vs multiplicative situations); M.PRF.2a pattern generalisation
misconceptions.description: Student adds a constant to both parts of a ratio instead of multiplying (e.g. 2:3, 4:5 instead of 4:6).
misconceptions.example_wrong_reply: 2:3 then 4:5 because I added 2 to each.
misconceptions.prompt_cue: You find the pattern by adding the same number each time, just like in a number sequence.

misconceptions.source: DLM M.EE.6.RP.1 — Successor linkage
misconceptions.description: Student doubles the first term but forgets to double the second (4:3 instead of 4:6).
misconceptions.example_wrong_reply: I multiplied 2 by 2 to get 4. I left the 3 alone. So 4:3.
misconceptions.prompt_cue: You remember to scale one number but forget both parts have to be scaled the same way.

misconceptions.source: LPF M.PRF.1e — representing and computing unit rates
misconceptions.description: Student divides in the wrong direction (hours/miles instead of miles/hours).
misconceptions.example_wrong_reply: 3 divided by 150 equals 0.02.
misconceptions.prompt_cue: You pick a division direction without thinking about what the unit rate means. You just pick the smaller divided by the bigger.

misconceptions.source: LPF M.NO.3a — justifying solutions; M.PRF.1e unit rates (6.RP-2)
misconceptions.description: Student computes the correct number but drops the unit (writes 50 instead of 50 miles/hour).
misconceptions.example_wrong_reply: 150 divided by 3 equals 50.
misconceptions.prompt_cue: You do the maths correctly but you don't think about what the number means or what units it has.

misconceptions.source: Emotional modeling — anxious/shutdown persona
misconceptions.description: Student says they don't know where to start and shuts down without attempting.
misconceptions.example_wrong_reply: I don't even know where to start. Can we skip it?
misconceptions.prompt_cue: You feel overwhelmed and just give up, saying you don't understand.

misconceptions.source: LPF M.NO.2d — contrasting situations as additive or multiplicative; phone-plans PST scenario
misconceptions.description: Student treats '$0.10 per text' as adding 10 cents once (a flat amount) instead of a constant rate times number of texts.
misconceptions.example_wrong_reply: Plan A is just 20 dollars plus 10 cents, so like 20.10 total.
misconceptions.prompt_cue: You hear '10 cents per text' and add 10 cents once instead of multiplying by how many texts.

misconceptions.source: LPF M.PRF.1e — unit rates in like or different units; phone-plans PST scenario
misconceptions.description: Student writes 10x instead of 0.1x (or 30x instead of 0.3x), confusing cents with dollars in the rate.
misconceptions.example_wrong_reply: Plan A is 20 + 10x because each text is 10 cents.
misconceptions.prompt_cue: You use 10 instead of 0.1 because the problem said ten cents, and you forget dollars.

misconceptions.source: LPF M.PRF.1c — comparing two rates for best value; phone-plans PST scenario
misconceptions.description: Student compares plans at one or two text counts and never sets them equal to find the crossover.
misconceptions.example_wrong_reply: At 50 texts Plan B is cheaper, so Plan B is always better.
misconceptions.prompt_cue: You pick a few numbers and decide from those, without finding when the two plans cost the same.

misconceptions.source: LPF M.PRF.1c / PST Maya — table comparison without warrants
misconceptions.description: Student concludes Plan B is cheaper from a table of values up to about 50 texts but cannot explain why the pattern holds or connect the table to equations.
misconceptions.example_wrong_reply: I made a table up to 50 texts and Plan B is cheaper. Like at 50 it's $15 and Plan A is $25. So... Plan B.
misconceptions.prompt_cue: You used a table up to about 50 texts ($15 vs $25) and pick Plan B, but you cannot explain why or write the equations.

misconceptions.source: LPF M.PRF.1f — symbolic expressions tied to the quantitative relationships in a situation; phone-plans PST scenario
misconceptions.description: Student can write 20+0.1x and 0.3x but cannot explain what 0.1 or 0.3 means in context (calls them 'the coefficient').
misconceptions.example_wrong_reply: It's 20 plus 0.1x. The 0.1 is just the coefficient.
misconceptions.prompt_cue: You can write the equation but you don't know what the 0.1 means in the phone plan story.

misconceptions.source: LPF M.NO.2d — fixed amount not separated from per-unit rate; phone-plans PST scenario
misconceptions.description: Student models Plan A as only 0.1x (or only the per-text rate) and forgets the $20 monthly fee.
misconceptions.example_wrong_reply: Plan A is just 0.1 times texts, same idea as Plan B but cheaper per text.
misconceptions.prompt_cue: You forget the $20 monthly fee and only use the per-text part for Plan A.

misconceptions.source: LPF M.PRF.1c — evaluating two rates for a given situation; phone-plans PST scenario
misconceptions.description: Student concludes Plan A is always better because $0.10/text is less than $0.30/text, ignoring when the monthly fee makes Plan A more expensive.
misconceptions.example_wrong_reply: Plan A is always better because ten cents is less than thirty cents per text.
misconceptions.prompt_cue: You only compare the per-text prices and decide the cheaper rate always wins.

misconceptions.source: LPF M.SE.1f — expressions that correspond to the given situation; phone-plans PST scenario
misconceptions.description: Student assigns Plan A's rate to Plan B or vice versa (e.g. Plan A = 0.3x, Plan B = 20+0.1x).
misconceptions.example_wrong_reply: Plan A is 0.3x and Plan B is 20 plus 0.1x... I think I mixed them up but whatever.
misconceptions.prompt_cue: You mix up which plan has the monthly fee and which has the higher per-text rate.

misconceptions.source: LPF M.PRF.2d — solving linear equations and explaining the reasoning; phone-plans PST scenario
misconceptions.description: Student sets 20+0.1x = 0.3x but solves incorrectly (e.g. concludes x=20 or x=50 instead of 100).
misconceptions.example_wrong_reply: 20 plus 0.1x equals 0.3x, so x is 20 texts.
misconceptions.prompt_cue: You know to set the plans equal but you mess up the algebra and get the wrong crossover.

misconceptions.source: LPF M.NO.2d — fixed amount attributed to a situation that does not have one; phone-plans PST scenario
misconceptions.description: Student adds a $20 fee to both plans or invents a fee for Plan B that is not in the problem.
misconceptions.example_wrong_reply: Both plans have like a 20 dollar fee, then Plan A adds 0.1x and Plan B adds 0.3x.
misconceptions.prompt_cue: You put a monthly fee on both plans even though only Plan A has one.

misconceptions.source: LPF M.PRF.1e — rates measured in like or different units; phone-plans PST scenario
misconceptions.description: Student treats $0.10 / $0.30 as a monthly charge or total bill piece rather than a per-text rate.
misconceptions.example_wrong_reply: Plan A is 20 plus another 0.10 for the month, and Plan B is just 0.30 for the month.
misconceptions.prompt_cue: You treat the 10 cents and 30 cents like monthly amounts, not costs that grow with each text.

misconceptions.source: LPF M.PRF.1b — distinguishing linear from nonlinear (and proportional) relationships in tables and graphs
misconceptions.description: Student assumes every plan scales like a ratio table: doubling the number of texts doubles the bill, which is false whenever there is a monthly fee.
misconceptions.example_wrong_reply: If 50 texts costs $25 on Plan A, then 100 texts costs $50.
misconceptions.prompt_cue: You scale the whole bill up and down like a ratio table, because that is how every rate problem has worked so far.

misconceptions.source: LPF M.PRF.2b — relating representations and identifying functions as linear or nonlinear
misconceptions.description: Student draws or describes both plans as lines through (0, 0), so a plan with a monthly fee has no starting value at zero texts.
misconceptions.example_wrong_reply: Both lines start at zero and Plan A just goes up slower.
misconceptions.prompt_cue: You picture every graph starting at the corner at zero, so a starting fee has nowhere to go on your line.
